newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Moroccan parties welcome parliamentary laws.
newsitem.headline: Moroccan parties welcome parliamentary laws.

text.p: Moroccan opposition parties on Monday welcomed the adoption at the weekend of two new laws shaping the future bicameral parliament ahead of elections expected to be held next month.

"Overall we are satisfied because several amendments we proposed were accepted but our main demand, which was for a two-round election for the upper house, was rejected," said a spokesman for the Socialist Union of People's Forces (USFP).
Parliament on Sunday unanimously adopted laws setting the number of MPs at 325 in the lower house and 270 in a new upper house.
Voters in the North African country last year overwhelmingly approved a constitutional referendum to create two houses, to replace the single 333-seat existing parliament.

M'hamed el Khalifa, spokesman for the old-guard Istiqlal party which is part of the four-party Koutla opposition bloc, said on Monday that his party voted for the change although two amendments it wanted were also rejected.
He said the group had proposed that indelible ink be used to mark voters' hands so they they could not vote twice, and party symbols should be adopted instead of colours on voting papers.
He also deplored the rejection of the Koutla proposal for a two-round election for the upper house.
The lower house, to be called the Chamber of Representatives, will be elected directly, while the new upper house, the Chamber of Counsellors, will be indirectly elected.
Local councils will elect 60 percent of the seats in the upper house. Professional bodies such as the chambers of agriculture, and of trade and industry, will decide the remainder.
The upper house will have power to force a non-confidence vote in the government. Officials say it will also help ensure development in rural areas, home to 50 percent of Morocco's 27 million people.
Morocco's main opposition parties have long criticised the present parliamentary system under which two thirds of the 333 MPs are elected by direct ballot and one third by an electoral college.

The official news agency MAP quoted Interior Minister Driss Basri as saying that the law under which candidates had to put down a 2,000 dirhams ($205) deposit, repayable if they obtained at least five percent of votes, would be maintained.

Earlier this month, King Hassan replaced 20 ministers with party affiliations, telling them it was better they be freed to focus on campaigning for elections. They were replaced by a smaller team, including for the first time four women secretaries of state.
Prime Minister Abdellatif Filali, who has no political ties and who is also foreign minister, remained in his posts, as did the interior minister.
